name: Black salve

card.summary: A dark escharotic paste, usually made with bloodroot and zinc chloride, that people apply to skin growths such as moles, tags and lesions in the hope of removing them without a clinic visit.
card.aka: Bloodroot salve, black drawing salve, escharotic paste, Cansema
card.note: Corrosive to normal skin as well as growths; dermatologists and regulators report scarring, disfigurement and missed or progressing cancers.

quick.overview:
Black salve is a topical escharotic: a paste that chemically destroys the skin it touches and leaves a dead scab (an eschar). People in alternative-health circles use it at home on moles, skin tags, cysts and other lesions, with the appearance goal of making a visible growth fall off without surgery.

Proponents describe it as a natural treatment that targets only abnormal tissue. Published reviews, which are mostly case reports and laboratory work, describe the paste as damaging to healthy and abnormal tissue alike, with scarring as a common outcome and no controlled clinical trials of cosmetic or curative results.
quick.how: Products are sold as tins or jars of dark paste online, often under names like drawing salve. Users describe dabbing it onto a single lesion, covering it, and waiting weeks for a scab to form and lift away, leaving an open wound that heals gradually.
quick.risks: Case reports describe pain, ulceration, infection, permanent scars, loss of tissue (including parts of the nose) and cancers that persisted or spread after treatment. Regulators in the US and Australia have issued warnings, and sale is illegal in Australia. Dermatology bodies advise having any new or changing lesion examined before it is treated.

lead: Black salve is a corrosive herbal-style paste, typically built around bloodroot (Sanguinaria canadensis) and often zinc chloride, that is applied to the skin to destroy a lesion. It belongs to the escharotics, pastes that burn tissue and leave a scab-like eschar [3][12].

In appearance terms, people use it on moles, skin tags, warts, cysts and other visible growths, hoping the lesion will slough off and leave clearer skin without an excision. Vendors promote it as natural and selective for abnormal cells, and testimonials circulate on alternative-health sites and social media [4][12].

Published literature consists mainly of reviews and case reports. They describe indiscriminate tissue destruction, frequent scarring or disfigurement, and cases where the underlying cancer persisted [2][3][4][7]. Regulators including the US FDA and Australia's TGA have warned against it [13].

chain: Paste applied to a visible lesion
Tissue is chemically destroyed and forms a scab
Scab lifts off, leaving a healed area where the growth was
angle.text: Users apply it to moles, tags and other blemishes hoping to remove them at home. Published case reports describe the resulting wound as often leaving a scar or deformity larger than the original lesion.

infobox: Sale illegal in Australia; FDA warnings in the US

paras: Black salve has no standard formula. Many products combine bloodroot extract with zinc chloride and fillers, and reviews note that the corrosive activity comes from sanguinarine and zinc chloride rather than the inert base [3]. Sanguinarine is the main alkaloid of bloodroot and is toxic to animal cells, which is the basis of the eschar it produces [15].
Products appear under many labels, including drawing salve and bloodroot ointment, and are sold through independent websites and online marketplaces [12].

Bloodroot was used traditionally in North America, and escharotic pastes were part of mainstream skin treatment in the 19th century, including a bloodroot and zinc paste sold by the surgeon Jesse Fell from 1850 [13]. Frederic Mohs used a related zinc chloride paste in the 1930s, work that led to Mohs micrographic surgery [13].

Modern black salve marketing grew with the internet. In 2008 the FDA sent a warning letter to a seller, in 2009 it listed Cansema among products described as fake cancer cures, and in 2012 the TGA advised Australians against black and red salves [13].

Vendors and users say the salve pulls out or kills only abnormal cells, is natural, and leaves little scarring. A review of vendor claims examined natural credentials, tumour specificity and cosmetic outcome, and concluded from laboratory and histology data that the paste probably harms normal tissue, while some cancer cell lines appear relatively resistant [4].

No controlled clinical trials have tested black salve. The clinical literature is case reports and series, which report suboptimal therapeutic and cosmetic outcomes [2][3]. A series of 16 cases examined pathology after application [16]. One case study described a thin melanoma treated with the salve that persisted and later metastasised [5], and other reports describe deformity after self-treatment [6][7].

Laboratory work indicates that sanguinarine destroys healthy skin cells at concentrations above about 5 micromolar [2]. Reviews have also examined theoretical risks including epidemic dropsy and carcinogenic potential of sanguinarine, neither of which has been established from black salve use [9][10].

Documented problems include pain, ulcers that heal over months, infection, scarring, loss of tissue, and treatment failure with later spread of a cancer [3][5][6]. A case report describes use on a neck cyst with significant tissue damage [11]. Because the paste cannot be controlled in depth, dermatology reviews describe it as dangerous without medical supervision [3]. The American Academy of Dermatology urged people to see a dermatologist before using home remedies for skin cancer [13].

Sale of black salve is illegal in Australia and the TGA has issued consumer warnings; the FDA has issued warning letters and public notices in the United States [8][13]. Sellers often label products for non-cancer uses such as drawing out splinters [12].

lore.intro: In alternative-health and some DIY-skin communities, black salve is discussed as a way to remove moles, tags and lesions at home, often alongside distrust of conventional dermatology [4][12].

claims.claim: Black salve kills only cancerous or abnormal cells and leaves healthy skin intact
claims.believers: Vendors and users say the paste selectively draws out abnormal tissue and cite personal testimonials [4].
claims.experts: Reviews of laboratory and pathology data report that sanguinarine and zinc chloride damage normal tissue and that some cancer cells resist the paste [2][4].

claims.claim: It removes moles and growths without scarring
claims.believers: Proponents say lesions fall out cleanly as a plug and heal naturally [4].
claims.experts: Case reports and reviews describe scarring, ulceration and disfigurement, including loss of tissue [3][6][7].

claims.claim: It is a safe natural alternative to surgery for skin cancer
claims.believers: Sellers promote it as natural and equivalent to orthodox treatment [4].
claims.experts: Reviews report no clinical trials and cases of persistent or metastatic disease after use; regulators have issued warnings [2][5][13].
